title: Rig — Compute
description: CPU and GPU, together first: which end the work is stuck at, then each processor in depth. Per-thread CPU occupancy, the full mode split, GPU engines, VRAM, clocks, power and the card's own throttle reasons.

panels.title: CPU busy
panels.description: Averaged over every thread. On its own it cannot tell one saturated core from every core half busy.

panels.title: Busiest thread
panels.description: The hottest single thread. Pinned at 1.0 while the average sits low is a single-threaded section, and it is what usually starves a GPU.

panels.title: GPU memory bus
panels.description: Time the memory controller moved data. Above the shader figure means the card is waiting on its own VRAM, and more shader clock will not help.

panels.title: Busy: CPU against GPU
panels.description: The four readings that decide which end the work is stuck at. Both high: the machine is working. GPU high, CPU low: GPU bound, and the CPU has nothing to do. GPU low with the busiest thread pinned: the GPU is starved by one thread feeding it. Both low with the load average up: neither processor is the problem — look at Storage.

panels.title: Memory: RAM against VRAM
panels.description: The two pools behave differently under pressure. RAM overcommits into swap and the machine gets slow. VRAM has no swap and no OOM killer: the driver refuses the allocation and the client that asked for it dies, compositor included.

panels.title: Clock, as a share of maximum
panels.description: Neither line reaches 1.0 under an all-core or all-SM load, so read the trend, not the value. Both falling together is one power or thermal envelope holding both parts down.

panels.title: Power and heat
panels.description: Mixed units on one axis on purpose: the question is whether power and temperature move together, not what either is worth. Thermals has the calibrated version.

panels.title: CPU cores held, by process group
panels.description: Pair this with the GPU panel beside it — the crosshair is shared across the board, so hovering names the group that was running when the GPU rose or fell.

panels.title: GPU engines
panels.description: A screen recorder or a video call lives on the encoder line and costs almost no shader time.

panels.title: Every thread
panels.description: One line per hardware thread. A flat band of lines at the same height is a parallel build; one line alone at the top is a section that cannot be split.

panels.title: Threads above 90%
panels.description: The same picture as one number. Equal to the thread count means the CPU is genuinely full; 1 means one thread is, and the other twenty-three are waiting for it.

panels.title: Time by mode
panels.description: The full split, not the three the Overview shows. A large system band is syscall or page-fault cost rather than the program's own work; a large interrupt band is a device, usually the network.

panels.title: Load average, split
panels.description: Only the runnable half is a CPU problem. The blocked half belongs to Storage.

panels.title: Clock
panels.description: Averaged over every thread, so a boosting core and a parked one blend. Falls under an all-core load by design, and again under heat.

panels.title: Pressure: CPU
panels.description: The share of time at least one runnable task was waiting for a thread. Rises before busy_ratio saturates, which makes it the earlier warning.

panels.title: Context switches by process group
panels.description: Scheduling churn. A group high here and low on cores held is spending its time being descheduled, not computing.

panels.title: Threads by process group
panels.description: Thread counts far above the CPU's own is where the context switches come from.

panels.title: Top CPU now (cores held)
panels.description: Cores, not percent. 4.0 is four threads solid.

panels.title: Scaling governor
panels.description: Threads under each governor. `schedutil` ramps on demand and lags a short burst; `performance` holds the clock up and costs idle watts. A split between two of them is a machine that was reconfigured half way.

panels.title: VRAM free
panels.description: What the next allocation has to fit in.

panels.title: Power against limit
panels.description: At 1.0 the card is clock-limited by its power budget, which is normal under load and is the commonest reason the clock sits below maximum.

panels.title: Throttle headroom
panels.description: Degrees before the card slows itself down.

panels.title: Throttled
panels.description: Total share of time any reason held the clock down. The panel below says which.

panels.title: VRAM
panels.description: Used is counted as installed minus free, which is the number the driver allocates against. nvidia-smi's own 'used' excludes its reserve, so it stops short of the total by a few hundred MiB even on a card that is refusing allocations.

panels.title: Why the clock is not at maximum
panels.description: Share of wall time each reason held the clock down, from the card's own counters rather than a 15-second sample of a flag. `power cap` is ordinary under load. `thermal` means the cooler, and Thermals says whether that is dust. `power brake` is the PSU asserting a hardware line and is never ordinary.

panels.title: Clocks
panels.description: Memory clock steps between a handful of fixed levels; shader clock is continuous. The memory clock dropping to its lowest step is the card deciding it is idle.

panels.title: Power
panels.description: Draw pressed flat against the limit for minutes is a power-limited card, not a broken one. `nvidia-smi -pl` moves the limit line.

panels.title: Temperature against power
panels.description: Rising temperature at equal power and equal fan is the cooler getting worse. Thermals turns this into a month-over-month ratio.

panels.title: Link to the host
panels.description: Both drop on an idle card to save power, so only a low reading while the GPU is busy means anything. A card stuck at half width under load is seated wrong or sharing lanes with an NVMe drive.

panels.title: Encoder sessions
panels.description: Screen recording, streaming and video calls. Latency climbing while the session count holds is the encoder queue backing up.

panels.title: Integrated GPU
panels.description: Read through DRM rather than nvidia-smi. Non-zero here means something is rendering on the integrated GPU, which for a desktop session is usually a mistake.

defaults.noValue: The integrated GPU is idle — the desktop is running on the discrete card.
